questions.stem: At what rate does the Reserve Bank of India pay interest to commercial banks when they park their surplus funds with the RBI on an overnight basis?

options.option_text: Repo rate, applied when banks borrow from RBI
Reverse repo rate, paid when banks lend to RBI
Bank rate, for long-term advances to scheduled banks
MSF rate, set above repo for emergency bank funds

questions.explanation: B is correct: the reverse repo rate is the rate at which RBI borrows from commercial banks — banks earn this rate when parking surplus funds with RBI. Option A is wrong because the repo rate is what banks pay when they borrow from RBI under a repurchase agreement, not what they earn by depositing funds.

questions.stem: Which borrowing window allows commercial banks to obtain overnight funds from the Reserve Bank of India by pledging eligible government securities, at a rate typically higher than the repo rate?

options.option_text: Liquidity Adjustment Facility repo auction window
Marginal Standing Facility emergency borrowing window
Standing Deposit Facility overnight absorption window
Export Credit Refinance penal-rate bank lending window

questions.explanation: B is correct: the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), introduced in 2011, lets scheduled commercial banks borrow overnight from RBI at repo + 25 basis points against eligible SLR-qualifying securities. Option C (SDF) is a common distractor — the Standing Deposit Facility is an absorption tool (banks park money with RBI), not a borrowing window.

questions.stem: Under banking regulations, which specific RBI rate serves as the benchmark for computing the penal interest charged on a commercial bank that fails to maintain the mandatory Statutory Liquidity Ratio on any given day?

options.option_text: Repo rate, applied on the SLR shortfall amount daily
Bank rate, plus a 3% penal surcharge on the SLR shortfall
Reverse repo rate, as SLR default reduces liquidity absorption
MSF rate, since banks dip into SLR securities at MSF window

questions.explanation: B is correct: under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, a bank failing to maintain SLR must pay penal interest at 3% above the Bank Rate on the daily shortfall amount. Option D is the most tempting distractor — MSF does allow banks to use SLR securities as collateral for borrowing (a different provision), which is entirely separate from the penalty for failing to maintain SLR.

questions.stem: Which RBI-mandated lending rate framework, effective from April 2016, replaced the 'Base Rate' system and compelled banks to price loans based on the incremental cost of their liabilities rather than the average cost?

options.option_text: Prime Lending Rate system based on average deposit costs
Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR)
External Benchmark-linked Lending Rate (EBLR) system
Treasury Bill-linked floating rate benchmark system

questions.explanation: B is correct: MCLR, effective April 2016, required banks to compute lending rates based on marginal cost of funds, CRR cost, and operating expenses — making monetary policy transmission faster than the Base Rate. Option C (EBLR) is a common confusion — the External Benchmark system (linking loans to repo rate or T-bill rate) came later in October 2019, applicable to new floating-rate retail and MSME loans.

questions.stem: Under RBI's Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms, what is the minimum percentage of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) that domestic scheduled commercial banks must mandatorily direct to priority sector borrowers?

options.option_text: 32% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit per annum
40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit per annum
35% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit per annum
25% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit per annum

questions.explanation: B is correct: domestic scheduled commercial banks (and foreign banks with 20+ branches) must direct 40% of ANBC to priority sectors including agriculture, MSMEs, education, and housing. Option D (25%) is the most tempting distractor — candidates often confuse this with sub-targets, but no individual sub-target is 25%; the agriculture sub-target is 18% of ANBC (with 10% for small and marginal farmers).

questions.stem: The Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), jointly established by the RBI and the Government of India in 2004, was designed to address which macroeconomic challenge, and what structurally distinguishes it from conventional Open Market Operations?

options.option_text: Controls domestic inflation; OMO is market-driven while MSS is RBI-directed lending
Sterilises capital-inflow rupee surplus; MSS proceeds go to a ringfenced RBI account
Manages forex reserve levels; MSS involves direct RBI bond issuance to the public
Regulates credit growth; MSS uses only T-Bills while OMO uses only dated securities

questions.explanation: B is correct: MSS was created to sterilise excess rupee liquidity from large foreign capital inflows that caused undue rupee appreciation. Unlike conventional OMO (where proceeds supplement government revenues), MSS bond/T-bill proceeds are held in a separate ringfenced MSS Cash Account with RBI and cannot be used for government expenditure — this prevents fiscal expansion while absorbing liquidity. Option D is wrong because MSS uses both T-bills and dated securities, and so does OMO.

questions.stem: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), operationalised by the RBI in April 2022 as the new floor of the LAF corridor, has one critical structural difference from the earlier reverse repo window. Which feature gives SDF superior flexibility as a liquidity absorption tool?

options.option_text: SDF provides RBI with a tool to inject fresh liquidity into the banking system daily
SDF absorbs bank funds with no government securities provided as collateral by RBI
SDF replaces both repo and reverse repo, making the LAF a single corridor rate
SDF operates exclusively on non-RTGS days to absorb weekend surplus liquidity

questions.explanation: B is correct: the SDF is an uncollateralised absorption facility — banks deposit surplus funds with the RBI without receiving government securities in return. In contrast, reverse repo required the RBI to provide G-secs as collateral, capping absorption at RBI's available G-sec holdings. SDF removes this ceiling, giving RBI unlimited sterilisation capacity. Option A is wrong — SDF is purely an absorption tool; the repo window handles liquidity injection.
